The reason people only doom about CS is because everyones worried about "me, me, me". They have tunnel vision. They're worried about their careers, and what's going to happen to them. So they're imagining a world where CS disappears, and the rest of the world goes completely unchanged, the economy doesn't crash, other fields still hire like normal, and life goes on for everyone else except us.

They're not zooming out and understanding that this is an everyone problem. Not just the careers that're cooked because of AI either. I mean everyone. When the 70+ million white collar employees in the US are all unemployed and trying to pivot out of their failing industry.... where do you think they're all going to go?

They're going to flood the trades, and jobs that currently aren't susceptible to AI.

Those fields do not have the room to support 70+ million people. Those fields will all become extremely oversaturated, and will crumble as well, just for an indirect reason.

This isn't a problem you and I are going to solve. This isn't a problem you're going to dodge by becoming a crab fisherman.

This is a problem that society is going to have to solve. It's going to change society as we know it. So buckle in and enjoy the ride. In the mean time, focus on what's in your control. I have a job now. I'm doing well at work now. I'm collecting a paycheck now. If any of that changes in the future, I'll make an educated decision about what to do next, based on what's happening in the world at that time. I'm not going to pre-emptively ditch an industry I've worked in for 13 years because some redditor says I'm doomed.

Medicine has an inherent physical aspect to it, so not sure about that. But law is just as impacted as we are by AI. Yes there's licensure, but that doesn't mean lawyers aren't using AI. I'm close friends with a lawyer who's been practicing for about 13 years. AI has completely changed his day to day. For example, he used to have his junior associates read through an insane amount of pages of case law, and provide him a summary relevant to a case he's working. He'd obviously have to review their work, check their claims, etc. He can't just blindly trust a green lawyer. But they do the grunt work, and he's focused on the bigger picture.

What he and the other experienced lawyers have been able to do with AI is have AI do the exact same thing that they used to have their junior associates do. Main difference is AI ends up providing significantly better summaries than the junior associates ever could. He still has to review everything, he still has to fact check everything, just like he did when he had human underlings providing him these things, so his workflow hasn't really changed. What's happening beneath him has changed dramatically.

Direct quote from him: "Associates are fucked". And that was a few years ago. I'm sure they're even more fucked now.

I'm sure parts of medicine are changing in similar ways. There obviously still needs to be a human involved, but I bet AI is augmenting the field to the point they no longer need people doing "grunt work". For a lot of these regulated fields the concern isn't AI just completely eliminating the field. The concern is AI wipes out the need for entry level people. Just like our concern.

text:
It's an interesting and somewhat bitter question. I think there are several reasons why computer science might be particularly hard hit by AI. However, contrary to popular belief, I don't think the main reason is that current models are inherently better at computer science tasks than at tasks in other white-collar jobs, whether because of the availability of open-source code, tighter training and feedback loops, or anything along those often-invoked lines.

One major factor is simply that many other professions aren't fully digital yet. Their workflows may involve looking things up in physical documents, dealing with paperwork, navigating fragmented IT systems requiring authorization, or any number of other mundane obstacles that make AI integration difficult. Software engineering, by contrast, is already a highly digital profession, and developers tend to be technologically inclined early adopters who experiment with these tools without needing much encouragement or instruction.

As a result, deploying AI in a software engineering organization may require little more than management giving the green light. In other white-collar professions, achieving comparable adoption might first require extensive digitization projects, workflow automation, employee training, organizational restructuring, and so on. The difference in impact may therefore have much more to do with the ease of deploying AI than with differences in its underlying capabilities.

Another important factor is how difficult it is to demonstrate that a model can actually perform at a high level in a given field.

In computer science and mathematics, results are often relatively easy to verify, or at least there are well-defined criteria for correctness. This is partly why we have things like the Millennium Prize Problems. Where are the equivalents in law, accounting, or other white-collar professions? I'm sure these fields have plenty of difficult and unresolved questions, but I suspect many are not the kind where a model could produce an answer and everyone would agree, "Well, that's it. The problem has been solved."

Instead, the answer would likely be subject to debate, with experts offering conflicting interpretations and opinions. A model might produce the best answer that could reasonably be given, yet still face extensive criticism from scholars who simply disagree with its conclusions. And much of that criticism would likely be interpreted as evidence of AI errors, hallucinations, or "slop," rather than as a reflection of the ambiguity and disagreement inherent in the profession itself.

I've actually heard people invoke precisely this ambiguity as an argument for why AI won't be able to perform certain kinds of professional work. But that seems to overlook an obvious question: how do humans perform that work? If a field is genuinely ambiguous, with multiple defensible answers and no single objectively correct solution, why should that necessarily make it harder for AI? In some respects, it could even make the task easier, since there are multiple acceptable answers rather than one narrowly defined correct result.

Of course, this also means that assessments of AI capabilities are highly vulnerable to human biases. We can already see this happening in mathematics, arguably one of the most objectively verifiable disciplines. As models become capable of producing results that are increasingly difficult to dispute on technical grounds, some criticism shifts toward less measurable objections: the proofs are "slop," the work isn't "real mathematics," the model doesn't "actually understand" what it's doing, and so on.

Now imagine how much stronger these dynamics could be in fields where correctness is substantially more subjective and ambiguous.

My broader point is that we should be careful not to confuse how quickly AI is adopted with how capable it actually is at doing the work. Computer science may be among the first professions to experience major disruption not because AI is uniquely good at programming, but because software engineering is unusually well positioned to adopt, integrate, and objectively evaluate AI systems.

Personally, I think we're far from "cooked". I'm a senior leader at a large corp and have worked in tech for 20+ years.

The reason "coding" has seen such rapid adoption and LLMs show real benefit is two fold.

There is simply an absolute ton of data (code) and decades worth of understanding how to evaluate and verify it. Helping models during not just training but also reinfforcement learning.

It's a "technology" and enginners and technology departments are highly adaptive, we love to automate things, tinker, play. So all the deterministic code, harnesses and frameworks to overcome some of the limitations of LLMs are being built at a ridiculous rate for our domain.

So why don't I think we're cooked? Well firstly people are still a bit to hung up on what the world felt like during COVID, I've never seen hiring like that in my career and it was the most insane period of my life. Not only was I personally approached almost daily for jobs with simply silly salaries on the table but hiring and securing people was a nightmare. So we've had a massive correction on top of AI driving down junior demand and some recalibration of team sizes - but job postings are starting to recover slowly which will likely put us back to a level prior to COVID.

Second, AI has yet to really "diffuse" (god how I hate that word) outside of Tech. While I'm certainly realistic on the potential of LLMs due to their limitations, just like we've experienced in Tech there is a sheer mountain of software, harnesses and things that'll need to be built as it for each industry to actually make LLMs work reliabley enough in each domain.

Third. As LLMs begin to "diffuse" (arghhh) in other industries, the types of software or solutions that can be built now due to LLMs will be huge. There are simply so many things you'd never even think of building as you'd need millions and millions and an army of engineers writing rules engines and novel like length deterministic logic. They were just not economical viable. LLMs however opens up so many opportunities.

It's going to feel rough - purely as so many companies are investing like crazy in AI and the casualty of cashflow going down is going to be headcount and COVID correction and AI has given organisations the perfect cover to execute redundancies without it hiting share price or investor confidence - but I do foresee a continued and steady recovery to what will be an explosion in demand for tech resource.

Although in part some of this "reset" is good, every tom, dick, harry and jane went into Computer Science in last 10-20 years because "learn to code" was sold as this guranteed route to a higher income. When many had no real passion for technology, solving complex technical problems or building things. We could afford to lose some of those people as they infuriate me.
